title: How to Disable the AI Features in Gmail and Google Docs
gist: A how-to for removing Gemini from Google Docs and Gmail that doubles as documentation of Google's AI adoption-forcing playbook: a giant Gemini bar rolled out to staged user cohorts, an opt-out buried in Gmail settings that never mentions Docs and also kills spellcheck and smart compose, no user-level control at all on Workspace accounts, and a third-party Chrome extension that hides Google AI across Gmail, Docs, Drive, and search using CSS.

insights.claim: Tech companies are pushing AI features on unwilling users through added interface buttons and pop-up tool tips designed to convert incidental clicks into dedicated usage, rather than waiting for organic demand.
insights.speaker: Justin Pot
insights.so_what: Reported AI engagement metrics from incumbents are inflated by forced surface area, so treat headline usage numbers as distribution artifacts rather than demand evidence.
insights.quote: Have you noticed how desperate tech companies are to get you to use their artificial intelligence features, even if you don’t want to use them?

insights.claim: Google is rolling out the Gemini bottom bar in Docs to staged, non-uniform user cohorts — the author first saw it in April while others have never seen it and some only got it in recent weeks.
insights.speaker: Justin Pot
insights.so_what: Cohorted rollout means Google is A/B testing tolerance for intrusive AI surfaces; the pace of general availability signals what those tests showed.
insights.locator: Google Docs, for example, is rolling out a giant Gemini bar

insights.claim: Google has a history of undoing user-side changes like AI opt-outs, so any setting that currently removes Gemini from Docs should be treated as temporary rather than durable.
insights.speaker: Justin Pot
insights.so_what: Opt-out durability is the real question for enterprise AI governance — controls that can be silently revoked are not compliance controls.
insights.quote: Enjoy not being distracted while working on documents—for now, at least. Google has a history of undoing changes like this.
insights.locator: If you depend on these features in Gmail

insights.claim: The only personal-account toggle that removes Gemini from Google Docs lives in Gmail's General settings under 'Smart features' and does not mention Google Docs anywhere, making the control effectively undiscoverable.
insights.speaker: Justin Pot
insights.so_what: Cross-product opt-outs hidden in an unrelated app are a textbook dark pattern; regulators scrutinizing consent design will find this pattern actionable.
insights.quote: It’s worth noting that this box in Gmail’s settings doesn’t even mention Google Docs.
insights.locator: Open your Gmail account, then click the gear

insights.claim: Disabling Gmail's Smart features also removes grammar suggestions, autocorrect, smart compose, smart reply, nudges, and Gmail's own spellcheck, bundling genuinely useful utilities with the AI features a user wants gone.
insights.speaker: Justin Pot
insights.so_what: Bundling wanted utilities with unwanted AI raises the effective cost of opting out — a deliberate retention mechanism worth watching for in other AI rollouts.
insights.quote: turning this off disables a number of other AI-powered features in Gmail, including grammar suggestions, autocorrect, smart compose, smart reply, and nudges
insights.locator: It’s also worth noting that turning this off

insights.claim: Even after disabling Smart features, a Gemini button remains in the top-right corner of Google Docs, so the opt-out is partial rather than complete.
insights.speaker: Justin Pot
insights.so_what: No full opt-out exists through first-party settings, confirming AI surfaces are treated as non-removable product furniture.
insights.locator: The Gemini menu, the audio button

insights.claim: The Gmail Smart features toggle works for some users and not others, which is why the author recommends a browser extension as the only method that seems to work for everyone.
insights.speaker: Justin Pot
insights.so_what: Inconsistent first-party controls push users to third-party tooling, ceding the last-mile UX layer to extension developers.
insights.locator: There are a couple ways to stop things like the Gemini menu

insights.claim: On Google Workspace accounts issued by an employer, only the IT administrator can turn off AI features and individual users have no self-service control at all, unlike personal @gmail.com accounts.
insights.speaker: Justin Pot
insights.so_what: Enterprise AI exposure is decided at the admin tier, so Google's Gemini penetration in business depends on a small number of IT policy defaults rather than end-user preference.
insights.quote: So if you use Google Workspace at your job, only the IT team can turn off the AI features.

insights.claim: The Bye Bye Gemini Chrome extension uses CSS to render every Google AI surface invisible across Gmail, Docs, and Drive, and also strips AI Overviews from Google search results.
insights.speaker: Justin Pot
insights.so_what: A cottage industry of AI-suppression extensions is emerging as a measurable counter-signal to forced AI adoption, and it directly attacks search-monetization surfaces.
insights.quote: The extension uses CSS to render all of those things invisible in the browser. It also has the benefit of removing AI Overviews from Google search results!
insights.locator: there’s another option: the Bye Bye Gemini extension

insights.claim: The only working method to hide AI Overviews from Google search is a Chrome or Safari extension that forces every search into the 'Web' section, since Google provides no toggle for it.
insights.speaker: Justin Pot
insights.so_what: Google's refusal to offer an AI Overviews opt-out signals how central the surface is to search monetization and how it will defend it.
insights.locator: Now if only Google would make it a bit easier

insights.claim: The author's objection is to AI being crammed into every interface by default rather than to AI itself, noting many Google Docs users may prefer Claude, ChatGPT, or a locally hosted Ollama setup over Gemini.
insights.speaker: Justin Pot
insights.so_what: Model preference is unbundling from the productivity suite; incumbents that force a single assistant risk pushing power users to rival models at the app layer.
insights.quote: Plenty of Google Docs users may prefer Claude, ChatGPT, or a locally hosted Ollama setup to Google's Gemini.
insights.locator: I'm not necessarily opposed to AI
